concepts.title: Nature and Characteristics of Groups
concepts.definition: A group is an organised system of two or more interacting, interdependent individuals who share common motives, occupy role relationships and live by norms; this separates it from a crowd that gathers by chance with no structure or belongingness, an audience assembled to watch passively, a mob with one polarised purpose and impulsive homogeneous action, and a team whose members carry complementary skills, shared commitment and mutual accountability that produce positive synergy.
concepts.formula: group = two_or_more_members + interdependence + common_motives + roles + norms ; team = group + complementary_skills + mutual_accountability
concepts.key_idea: A dropped catch by one fielder punishes the whole team - that interdependence, not mere presence at one place, is what makes a family, class or playing set a true group.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy107.txt, What is a Group? (six salient characteristics, Fig 7.1 football team vs audience, crowd, mob, team differences)
question_patterns: define a group and list its salient characteristics in Class 12 social psychology

solution_steps.explain: perceived membership, common motives and goals, interdependence, mutual influence, interaction and role-norm structure mark a genuine group
crowds lack structure and belongingness, audiences stay passive, mobs act with polarised impulsive purpose, and teams add complementary skills with mutual accountability

worked_examples.q: How many members must a group have at minimum: two or ten?

concepts.title: Why People Join Groups
concepts.definition: Group membership pays in several currencies: security against the insecurity of being alone, status borrowed from a group others consider important, self-esteem and positive social identity from prestigious membership, satisfaction of psychological and social needs such as belongingness, attention, love and power, goal achievement that no individual could manage alone, and knowledge and information that widen one's view.
concepts.formula: join_reasons = security + status + self_esteem + psychological_social_needs + goal_achievement + knowledge_information
concepts.key_idea: Because different groups feed different needs, everyone holds several memberships at once - which is why competing demands and expectations press on us.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy107.txt, Why Do People Join Groups? (six reasons with school debate and slum teaching examples)
question_patterns: what motivated you to join a group you belong to - discuss the reasons the chapter names
how does group membership supply security and status to a member?
which joining reason explains the pride when your school wins an inter-institutional debate?
why can some goals be achieved only through groups rather than alone?
how do groups provide knowledge and information that an individual lacks?

solution_steps.explain: security, status, self-esteem, psychological and social needs, goal achievement, and knowledge or information are the chapter's list
simultaneous memberships create competing demands and expectations that members must usually manage

worked_examples.q: Borrowed importance from a prestigious membership supplies what: status or security?

concepts.title: Group Formation: Conditions and Tuckman's Stages
concepts.section: Group Formation / Stages of Group Formation
concepts.definition: Groups arise where contact and interaction are eased by proximity (same colony, school or playground), similarity (consistent, validating company whose views reinforce ours), and common motives or goals such as teaching slum children together. Tuckman then splits development into five stages - forming with uncertainty and excitement, storming with conflict over control and tasks until a leadership hierarchy appears, norming when behaviour norms and positive identity form, performing when the accepted structure drives the goal, and adjourning when a committee disbands after its function ends.
concepts.formula: formation_conditions = proximity + similarity + common_motives_goals ; tuckman_stages = forming + storming + norming + performing + adjourning
concepts.key_idea: Groups need not march through the stages neatly - some stages run together, some repeat, and some are skipped entirely.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy107.txt, Group Formation (three conditions, television-violence validation example), Stages of Group Formation, Activity 7.1 open house committee
question_patterns: how does Tuckman's stage model help in understanding the formation of groups?

solution_steps.explain: repeated nearby contact, validated similarity, and shared motives or goals start the group

solution_steps.action: check the stage sequence and its flexibility
solution_steps.explain: forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning normally follow in order, though real groups may overlap, reverse or skip stages

concepts.title: Group Structure: Roles, Norms, Status and Cohesiveness
concepts.definition: As members interact, a structure regularises the group through four elements: roles, the socially defined expectations attached to a position such as son, daughter or team captain; norms, the agreed and enforced standards or unspoken rules of behaviour and belief; status, the relative social position that may be ascribed by seniority or achieved by expertise and hard work; and cohesiveness, the togetherness, we-feeling and mutual attraction that makes members think and act as one unit and holds them in the group.
concepts.formula: structure_elements = roles + norms + status + cohesiveness ; status = ascribed or achieved
concepts.key_idea: The cricket captain outranks teammates in status though all matter equally; extreme cohesiveness, however, can breed groupthink.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy107.txt, four important elements of group structure (roles, norms, status, cohesiveness)
question_patterns: name the four elements of group structure and define each

solution_steps.explain: roles fix expected behaviour, norms set shared standards, status ranks members, and cohesiveness binds them into a we-feeling unit
status may be ascribed, as with seniority, or achieved through expertise and hard work, and it varies even inside one group

worked_examples.q: Socially defined expectations attached to a position are called what?

concepts.title: Groupthink and Its Prevention
concepts.definition: Groupthink, identified by Irving Janis, is the failure of extremely cohesive, like-minded groups whose concern for unanimity overrides realistic appraisal: everyone assumes consensus, dissent stays unspoken for fear of breaking cohesion, the group inflates its own power, and warnings from the real world are minimised - as when President Johnson's circle escalated the Vietnam War against advice. Countermeasures are rewarding critical thinking and disagreement, presenting alternative courses of action, inviting outside experts, and seeking feedback from trusted outsiders.
concepts.formula: groupthink_risk = high_cohesion + homogeneity + isolation + no_alternatives + high_cost_decision ; prevention = critical_thinking + alternatives + outside_experts + trusted_feedback
concepts.key_idea: The Vietnam escalation of 1964-67 cost 56000 American and over a million Vietnamese lives - the textbook price of unanimity pressure inside an isolated leadership group.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy107.txt, Box 7.1 Groupthink (Janis, consensus appearance, Vietnam War example, four preventive ways)
question_patterns: what is groupthink and why does extreme cohesiveness produce it?

solution_steps.explain: concern for unanimity overrides realistic appraisal, producing irrational, uncritical decisions cloaked in apparent consensus
critical thinking, alternative courses, outside experts and feedback from trusted others are the four counteractions

worked_examples.q: Who identified groupthink: Janis or Latane?

concepts.title: Types of Groups and Tajfel's Minimal Group Paradigm
concepts.definition: Groups come in contrasted types: primary groups like family, caste and religion are pre-existing, face-to-face and emotionally warm with impermeable boundaries, while secondary groups such as a political party are joined by choice with impersonal, infrequent ties; formal groups like a university spell out functions, rules and roles, unlike close informal groups; and the ingroup of 'we' is viewed favourably while the outgroup of 'they' is often perceived negatively. Tajfel's minimal group paradigm proved the point: British schoolboys grouped by mere preference for Kandinsky or Klee paintings still distributed money in favour of their own group.
concepts.formula: type_pairs = primary_vs_secondary + formal_vs_informal + ingroup_vs_outgroup ; minimal_group -> ingroup_favouritism
concepts.key_idea: Even a flimsy criterion with no past or future is enough to trigger favouritism, though such categories are created by us - and India's composite culture celebrates plurality instead.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy107.txt, Type of Groups (three pairs), Box 7.2 minimal group paradigm with the allocation matrix, Activity 7.2
question_patterns: compare and contrast formal and informal groups, and ingroups and outgroups
why are family and caste called primary groups while a political party is secondary?
what makes the boundary of a primary group less permeable than that of a secondary group?

solution_steps.explain: primary-secondary turns on given versus chosen membership, formal-informal on explicit rules and roles, ingroup-outgroup on we-versus-they categorisation
boys who knew their group only by painting preference and code numbers still favoured their own group, proving how little a category needs to bias behaviour

worked_examples.q: Family, caste and religion are which type of group: primary or secondary?

concepts.title: Social Facilitation and Social Loafing
concepts.section: Influence of Group on Individual Behaviour - Social Loafing
concepts.definition: Social facilitation shows that the presence of others arouses and can lift the performance of someone already good, provided individual effort is evaluated; but when outputs are pooled, as in tug-of-war, individuals work less hard - social loafing, the reduction in individual effort on a collective task that lets members become free riders. Latane's clapping and cheering experiments made the point: total noise rose with group size of two, four and six, yet each participant's noise dropped as the group grew, because responsibility diffuses, individual contribution goes unmeasured, comparison with other groups is absent, coordination is poor, and membership alone does not matter to members. Loafing shrinks when each person's effort is identifiable, pressure to work hard rises, the task gains apparent importance, individual contribution is valued, and cohesiveness strengthens.
concepts.formula: effort_per_head = total_group_output / group_size ; loafing_gap = output_alone - effort_per_head
concepts.key_idea: Larger groups divide attention and responsibility, so the per-person share of effort falls even while the group total climbs.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy107.txt, Social Loafing (tug-of-war example, Latane noise experiments with groups of 2, 4 and 6, five causes, five reducers)
question_patterns: define social loafing and explain why it occurs in groups with pooled outputs

why does making each member's effort identifiable reduce free riding?
distinguish social facilitation from social loafing in terms of evaluated individual effort

compute the per-participant noise when a group of 4 makes a total of 48 units

solution_steps.action: divide the group's total output by the number of members
solution_steps.explain: pooled output hides individual contribution, so the average per member shows what each actually gave

solution_steps.action: subtract the per-head figure from the solo output
solution_steps.explain: the gap measures how much effort each member sheds while working in the group

worked_examples.q: The reduction in individual effort on a collective task is called social what?

concepts.title: Group Polarisation
concepts.definition: Group polarisation is the strengthening of a group's initial position through discussion, so that groups take more extreme decisions than individuals would - colleagues may let a bribed employee go scot-free or demand dismissal instead of a proportionate punishment. It happens because like-minded company supplies newer arguments for your view, the visible agreement of others acts as a bandwagon that validates the view as public opinion, and perceived ingroup membership breeds conformity that hardens the stance.
concepts.formula: polarisation = initial_position strengthened by group_discussion ; drivers = new_arguments + bandwagon_validation + ingroup_conformity
concepts.key_idea: Discussing capital punishment among supporters hardens both pro and anti camps - the danger is that positions may swing from very weak to very strong.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy107.txt, Group Polarisation (employee punishment example, capital punishment discussion, three reasons, Activity 7.3 attitude scale)
question_patterns: what is group polarisation and why do groups take extreme decisions?

how does identifying with an ingroup strengthen conformity to its view?

solution_steps.explain: whatever the group's initial stance, interaction and discussion push that stance to a stronger, more extreme version
newer arguments favouring the view, public validation through the bandwagon effect, and ingroup identification with conformity account for the hardening

worked_examples.q: Strengthening of a group's initial position through discussion is called group what?

worked_examples.problem: In a repetition of Latane's noise experiment, a group of 6 students clapping together produces a total of 60 units of noise, whereas a student clapping alone produces 15 units. Find the per-head output and the social loafing gap.

steps.action: divide total group output by group size
subtract the per-head figure from the solo output

worked_examples.answer: effort_per_head = 10 and loafing_gap = 5, so each member gives one-third less effort than when clapping alone

worked_examples.problem: A tug-of-war team of 4 pulls with a total force of 48 units. Working alone on a practice rope, each member had pulled 15 units. Compute the per-head force in the team and the loafing gap.

steps.action: divide the team total by the number of pullers
subtract the team per-head force from the solo pull

worked_examples.answer: effort_per_head = 12 and loafing_gap = 3 units of force lost per member - exactly the free-riding the chapter describes for pooled tasks
